Bhante Pannakara Meet and Greet: Mindfulness and Balance in Practice

On September 19, 2026, the Buddha Meditation Center of Greater Washington DC was grateful to welcome Bhante Pannakara for a warm evening of practice, reflection, and community. Friends gathered for Buddha Vandana chanting, a discussion of mindfulness, and dinner shared together.

An Evening of Practice and Community

The evening began with Buddha Vandana, a traditional form of chanting that offers an opportunity to recollect the qualities of the Buddha and settle the mind. It was followed by a conversation about mindfulness—not as an abstract idea, but as a way of meeting the thoughts and habits that shape our daily lives.

Gathering for dinner afterward gave everyone time to continue the conversation and enjoy one another’s company. These simple moments of practice and fellowship help strengthen the conditions that support the path.

Mindfulness and the Chaos We Create

During the discussion, Bhante Pannakara reflected on how many small unwholesome thoughts can create turmoil in the mind and in our lives. When these thoughts are not recognized, it can be difficult to feel settled or still.

Mindfulness offers a different response. We can learn to notice what is arising, pause before following every thought, and gradually let go of what is not helpful. This is not about blaming ourselves for having difficult thoughts. It is about seeing clearly and choosing, again and again, to cultivate what is wholesome.

[[internal link opportunity: mindfulness meditation]]

The Middle Way of Effort

A central teaching of the evening was the importance of balance in practice. Bhante Pannakara shared:

“If we put too little effort into our practice, we will not get far. But if we put too much effort without wisdom, we will break. You have to be in the middle and balance.”

This reminder speaks to a familiar challenge for many practitioners. When effort is too weak, mindfulness can fade and old habits can take over. When effort becomes strained, however, meditation can turn into another struggle. Wise effort is neither passive nor harsh. It is steady, patient, and responsive to what is happening in the present moment.

A mindfulness practice can begin with something simple: noticing the breath, recognizing a thought without immediately reacting to it, or returning attention to the body with kindness. Over time, these small moments can help us create less confusion and more peace in our daily lives.

We offer our sincere gratitude to Bhante Pannakara and to everyone who joined this meaningful gathering. May the mindfulness and balance cultivated together continue to support our practice. May all beings be well, happy, and peaceful. 🙏
